Pulling Company Financials Straight From SEC Filings. Free, No Vendor, No API Key. Three Routes Tested Head to Head.

3 min read
Just now

--

Spent a session in Claude Cowork pulling company financials straight from SEC filings, free, no vendor and no API key.
The setup that worked: edgartools Python library + edgartools Skills + SEC EDGAR API, run by an AI cowork app, Claude Cowork or ChatGPT Work.
Read free here
Am analyzing the free cash flows for the Mag 7 and wanted to dig into the line items and recategorize into my custom buckets. Tried out three routes on the same six quarters and seven companies, the SEC XBRL API directly, edgartools, and yfinance. All three agreed on the numbers. Where they split is coverage and traceability.
edgartools is the first call for most of this. The raw SEC API stays useful for screening thousands of filers in one go, and as a second path for checking. That checking earned its keep, the one number that disagreed turned out to be my own error, a restatement I had handled wrong.
edgartools is by Dwight Gunning, MIT licensed, past 2,000 stars, and it ships Claude skills and an MCP server: https://github.com/dgunning/edgartools
Read the full write-up
Covers the basics of SEC XBRL filings as well as a comparison of the approaches, in a FAQ manner and plain language. Every script, dataset and filing behind the numbers is linked from the page itself, so you can read the code that produced any figure.

How I built this document with Claude Cowork
I did not start with a plan to write anything. I started with the actual work, pulling free cash flows for the Mag 7 . Finance I understand but was getting confused with XBRL concepts as well as when to use SEC’s API vs. edgartools vs. Yahoo finance.
So I just asked Claude Cowork one question at a time, and each time I asked it to go and test it against real filings and put the answer on an HTML page I could read ….then the next question, and the page grew. That document is the conversation, built one question at a time, and every number on it came from a script that ran during the session rather than from the model’s memory.
And that’s how I do many of my analysis also with Claude Cowork.. one question at a time… report and validation to be shown as HTML … and final report packaged into a PDF
same should hold for any cowork apps including the recently released ChatGPT Work
On yfinance
It is an excellent library and I use it across my own apps, for pricing data, quick financial pulls and analyst recommendations. For this particular job, line item work with long history that has to trace back to a specific filing, it is the wrong tool. The write up has a section on where each one fits.
The larger point
Cowork app has become a universal frontend for this kind of work. Once you have API access, MCP and skills, connecting to almost any backend and running the whole analysis in one place is straightforward, and the same session can then turn it into a PDF, fit a statistical or machine learning model, or build the page you are looking at.
More on this on my hub page Claude for Analytics… same thing applies whichever AI Cowork apps you are using
